paras: The attempted lynching in Henderson County, North Carolina, was an attack in August 1903 in which five or six white men nearly lynched an unnamed Black man after a row over a belt trade. Some men from Asheville arrived and rescued him almost at the last moment, and a Raleigh correspondent reported the incident beside the state's count of lynchings for the year.

According to a Raleigh special dated August 22, the man and a white man had either swapped belts or talked of making such a trade. A row followed, though the report does not say who began it, where in the county it took place, or what was said.

Five or six white men who were "in the party" then set about lynching the man and were "on the point of" doing so. At that moment "some gentlemen from Asheville luckily appeared" and rescued him, in the correspondent's words "almost at the last moment." No injuries are reported, and neither the man nor any of the white men is named.
No report of arrests, charges or any official inquiry into the attempt appears in the coverage.

The only known account ran in the Atlanta Constitution on August 24, 1903, as a Raleigh special under the headline "Lynchings in North Carolina." It opened with the statement that the state had had only two lynchings that year, the last in Halifax County, and offered the Henderson County incident as one "very narrowly prevented."

reader.title: Attempted lynching in Henderson County, North Carolina (1903)
bases: Five or six white men were 'on the point of lynching' a Black man when others rescued him, an attempted lynching that did not end in a death (A1).
The man was rescued alive, so no one was killed; the group of five or six acted without any authority, but the only report gives no accusation or stated justification beyond a row over belts (A1).
Only one Raleigh special printed in the Atlanta Constitution describes the incident; a Wilmington paper's Raleigh letter of the same week does not mention it (A1, A2).
